blocks.intro: Leaks don't always drip where you can see them:

tiles.body: If your use hasn't changed and the bill has, water is going somewhere.

tiles.h3: The Meter Moves With Everything Off
tiles.body: Turn off every fixture and watch the meter. If it moves, there's a leak.

tiles.h3: Stains, Bubbling Paint or Soft Floors
tiles.body: Water inside a wall or under a floor shows up on the surface eventually.
Hidden moisture feeds mold. The smell often comes before the stain.

blocks.intro: From a pinhole to a full line:

steps.body: Copper pinholes, failed fittings and corroded galvanized pipe.
Leaks in the line from the meter to the house, found with listening and tracing equipment.
Toilets, supply lines, water heaters and washer hoses.
When galvanized pipe is rusting through in several places, replacing it beats patching one leak at a time.

blocks.intro: The age of your home says a lot about where a leak is likely to start.

items.body: Homes from the 1940s through the 1960s may still have galvanized steel supply lines. They rust from the inside, so leaks show up at threaded joints first, often in more than one place.
Copper is durable, but after 40 or 50 years some lines develop pinhole leaks, especially near fittings. One pinhole can mean others are coming.
The line from the street to your home is buried and out of sight. A wet patch in the yard or a meter that won't stop can point to a leak there.

items.h3: Winter Leaks That Start at Thaw
items.body: A pipe that froze and split in January often doesn't leak until it warms up. See [burst pipe repair](/arlington-heights/burst-pipe-repair).

blocks.h2: Leak Questions From Arlington Heights Homeowners

items.q: How do I check for a hidden leak?
items.preview: Turn off all water and watch the meter.
items.answer: Turn off every faucet and appliance that uses water, then look at your water meter. If it keeps moving, there's a leak somewhere. Call us and we'll find it.

items.q: Can you find a leak without opening walls?
items.preview: Usually we can pinpoint it first, so only a small opening is needed.
items.answer: Usually. We use moisture meters and listening equipment to find the spot first, so we open only a small area where the leak actually is.

items.q: Should I replace my galvanized pipes?
items.preview: If they're leaking or pressure is low, it's usually time.
items.answer: If you're seeing leaks at the joints, rusty water or low pressure, the pipe is near the end of its life. Replacing it ends the cycle of patching one leak after another. We'll show you what we find.

items.q: Is a small leak worth fixing right away?
items.preview: Yes. Small leaks cause mold and rot over time.
items.answer: Yes. A slow leak inside a wall can cause mold, rot and ceiling damage long before it's obvious. Fixing it early is almost always cheaper.

items.q: How much does leak repair cost in Arlington Heights?
items.preview: It depends on where the leak is and how we reach it. You get a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on where the leak is, what kind of pipe it's in and how we reach it. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins.
